stories.title: Jacob Johns of Hart Township: from Baltimore to Fort Blakely
stories.hook: At twenty Jacob Johns left a Winona County farm for the Sixth Minnesota Infantry, and ended up in the swamps of Arkansas and the last siege of the Civil War; he later fathered twelve children, one of whom married into the Rivers family.
body: Jacob Johns of Hart Township enlisted in Company E of the Sixth Minnesota Infantry on 15 August 1862. His 1895 biography gives his birth as 5 August 1842 in Germany, making him twenty at enlistment; the family tree instead gives 1840. He arrived in America as a young child after a two-month voyage to Baltimore. The family spent seven years in Missouri, moved to Hazel Green, Wisconsin, and settled in Hart Township in 1856.

His service included the battles of Birch Coulee on 2 September 1862 and Wood Lake on 23 September during the U.S.–Dakota War. The conflict brought severe losses and displacement to Dakota communities as well as deaths among soldiers and settlers. That December, thirty-eight Dakota men were executed at Mankato. The Sixth Minnesota remained on the frontier and took part in military expeditions into Dakota territory in 1863.

In June 1864 the Sixth Minnesota was sent to Helena, Arkansas, where disease devastated the regiment. By late September, 654 of its 950 men were reported sick, mostly with malaria. Jacob later served in the Mobile campaign at Spanish Fort and Fort Blakely in 1865. He completed his service as a private, without being wounded or taken prisoner, and was discharged on 19 August 1865.

He bought eighty acres in section 28 of Hart Township, which grew to 440. On 18 May 1868 he married Theresa (the book prints her surname as "Kryzer"). The twelve children were Mary, Sophia, Lizzie, Emma, Annie, Jacob, Henry, Rose, Willie, Hannah, Eddie and George. The family was Catholic, Jacob was a Democrat, and he served as township supervisor and constable and belonged to the Grand Army of the Republic.

Johanna Johns, who married Edward Rivers Sr. of Rollingstone on 22 June 1909, was born on 11 November 1888 at Rushford in Fillmore County, 'to Jacob and Theresa Johns.' She died at home in Rollingstone on 4 March 1967 and was buried at Holy Trinity Catholic Cemetery. She was survived by a brother, George, in Canada and a sister, Mrs. Rose Tiernan, in Albertville. Johanna is probably the Hannah of the 1895 list of children; the link rests on the parents' names, the sibling names and the location, and is not proven. Her marriage joined a German Catholic farm family to the Luxembourg Catholic Riverses, and both her father and her husband's uncle, John B. Rivers of the 48th Wisconsin, had worn Union blue.

The connection to Johanna has more than names behind it. The 1895 household contained seven daughters and five sons, including Hannah, Rose and George. Johanna's 1967 family notice names Rose and George as her surviving siblings and records five sisters and four brothers who had already died. Those counts fit the earlier household exactly. Together with Jacob and Theresa's names and the Rushford area, they make Hannah's identification as Johanna a strong possibility, though an original birth or marriage record is still needed to settle it.

stories.title: Wings in August, a parade in January
stories.hook: Two hometown newspaper items follow Bob Johnson from jump school in 1958 to the Kennedy inaugural parade in 1961.
body: In August 1958 Bob Johnson earned his parachutist wings at the 82nd Airborne Division Jump School at Fort Bragg, North Carolina. The course included five training jumps. He was twenty-one and only six months into his Army service, having entered that February and completed basic training at Fort Ord, California.

Before the Army, Bob attended Decatur Baptist College in Texas. His parents lived in different communities: his father Joel G. Johnson remained on the Boehler Route near Boswell, while his mother Nettie was then Mrs. Nettie B. McCarter of Sherman. Those family addresses accompanied the announcement of his airborne qualification.

Jump school at Fort Bragg was the gate to the Army's airborne divisions. The 82nd Airborne, headquartered there, was a Strategic Army Corps unit, which the Army described as ready to deploy anywhere on short notice.

By January 1961 Bob was a Specialist Four and a supply clerk in the Mortar Battery of the 504th Infantry, 82nd Airborne Division. He had served in Germany and was again based at Fort Bragg. That month he marched with his unit in President John F. Kennedy’s inaugural parade in Washington. At twenty-three, the 1957 Decatur High School graduate had already served on both sides of the Atlantic.

His mother's name changed in the three years between the items. In 1958 she is Mrs. Nettie B. McCarter of Route 2, Sherman; in 1961, Mrs. Nettie B. Tillery of Sadler, Texas. She had been Nettie Tyson, and the household she grew up in is told in the story of the two Tyson sisters. She died on 6 February 1980 and is buried at Sunnyside Cemetery in Savoy, Fannin County, Texas, her last residence.

These were the Army's own hometown releases, mailed from Fort Bragg to the papers in a soldier's home county, and the earliest published notice of a career that would run twenty years through Germany, Korea and Vietnam and end with a Warrant Officer 3's rank. Eleven months after the parade, on 21 December 1961, he married Margie Bell.

stories.title: A license in July 1938
stories.hook: The Choctaw County court docket records Opal Tyson's marriage license, the first step toward the Wilson, Johnson and Tyson household of 1940.
body: In July 1938 Opal Tyson and Seidel Wilson obtained a marriage license in Choctaw County, Oklahoma. The couple appeared among the Boswell marriage-license notices published that month in the Paris News and the Southeast Oklahoman. Opal was eighteen. A license documents the intention to marry; the notices do not supply a ceremony date.

By the spring of 1940 she was living as Opal Wilson at her father Albert Tyson’s rented farm in Oakes Township. With her was her infant son Don. Her sister Nettie Johnson and Nettie’s young son Bob were in the same household, alongside their parents and younger brother Marion.

Over the following decade, the children’s households changed. In 1950 Opal was enumerated as Joe Johnson’s wife, with Don as Joe’s stepson and Bob living with them. A later marriage between Opal Wilson and Joel Gilbert Johnson was recorded in Sevier County, Arkansas, on 3 December 1968. The earlier household and later marriage record are distinct events; they do not establish when the couple first began living together.

stories.title: The Rivers store and the families around it
stories.hook: John B. Rivers opened a Rollingstone store in 1872. His children carried on its trade, linking the Rivers, Heber and Jung families.
body: John B. Rivers, Henry Rivers’s brother, married Anna Heber on 29 October 1866, the same year he bought a farm in Norton Township. He opened a store in Rollingstone in 1872. Their children were John H., Matthew, John P., Elizabeth and Josephine. Anna’s father was Nicholas Heber.

John H. Rivers, born in Norton Township on 13 December 1867, studied at Winona State Normal School and a Winona business college before working with his father. He later ran a grocery in Winona with his brother John P. In 1896 he returned to Rollingstone and opened a general dry goods business. His brother Matthew, born at Rollingstone on 8 December 1874, stayed in the family general store and served as assistant postmaster. The brothers carried their father's work into a new generation.

John H. married Bertha Jung on 10 October 1894. Her parents, merchant John Jung and Margaretha Kohner, belonged to Rollingstone's 1855 settlers. Their children Andrew and Angeline were born on 10 December 1895 and 13 October 1899. The marriage linked two village business families, while their cousins continued the Rivers mail route.

stories.title: Sarah and George Hall: a Wabasha household
stories.hook: Pennsylvania, Iowa and Minnesota connect Sarah Butturff’s family to the Canfields of Kellogg.
body: Sarah Butturff was born in Cumberland County, Pennsylvania, in February 1825, a daughter of Frederick and Elizabeth. She married George W. Hall on 6 February 1849. George, born in Perry County in 1824, was the son of Moses and Catharine Hall. Their daughter Anna later married John A. Canfield of Kellogg.

George entered the grocery trade in Muscatine, Iowa, in 1854. Three years later, the family reached Wabasha, Minnesota, where he opened a furniture store with Sarah’s brother Samuel Butturff. A move to a Glasgow Township homestead in 1860 lasted three years; poor health brought George back to town. He worked as a store clerk and later kept a meat market.

By George’s death on 7 May 1870, the household owned two adjoining residences on Allegheny Street. Sarah still held them when the family biography was published in 1884. Anna had died by then. Her brothers Henry, William Parker and George connected the family to Greenfield, Minnesota, and Prairie View, Kansas.

stories.title: Five Williams brothers in one photograph
stories.hook: A family photograph identifies Cleave Williams with four brothers, linking the Tennessee-to-Texas family across five faces.
body: A family caption identifies the men in this formal photograph as John Arthur Williams and William at the back, with Arch, Cleave and George seated in front. White shirts, dark jackets and carefully arranged hands give the picture its studio formality. The surviving print is creased and torn, but all five faces can still be seen. Its date and photographer are unknown.

Their lives spread beyond the same household. Arch, born in Tennessee on 27 November 1871, came to Texas around 1891 and later made his home west of Tom Bean. He married Fannie Racer of Collinsville. At his death in 1938, his surviving brothers were Bud and Cleve at Van Alstyne and John at Dallas; his sisters lived in Van Alstyne, Hamlin, Brownfield and Sherman. The family had stayed connected while making homes across the state.

George, the youngest man in the front row, died on 31 May 1911 at twenty. His Van Alstyne marker records his birth on 1 February 1891. Cleave lived until 1949; through his daughter Melba and granddaughter Margie, his branch leads to Rachel. The photograph preserves the brothers together before the losses recorded on the cemetery stones.

stories.title: Katherine Rivers and the Reiland family
stories.hook: A Rivers daughter’s marriage connects teaching, shopkeeping and village service in Rollingstone.
body: Katherine Rivers, born on 21 March 1871, was a daughter of Henry Rivers and Elizabeth Lehnertz. On 20 August 1891 she married Michael N. Reiland. His parents, Peter Reiland and Christine Krier, had come from Luxembourg. They brought Michael from Wisconsin to Winona County in 1862, the year he was born, and developed a farm in Norton Township.

Michael studied in Winona and at St. Francis College in Milwaukee, then taught for twelve years in Winona’s public schools. In 1892 he moved into the dry-goods business at Rollingstone. Shopkeeping was only part of his village life: he also served as village clerk and school treasurer.

By 1913 Katherine and Michael had four children. Arthur taught school, while Leonard worked in the Rollingstone grocery trade. Adelaide attended a domestic-science school in Sparta, Wisconsin; Lorenda was still at home. Their lives place another Rivers household within the village’s schools and businesses, alongside the mail carrying, hotel keeping and retail work of their relatives.

stories.title: Audrey Johnson King: from Soper to Sterling City
stories.hook: Joel and Winnie Johnson’s daughter made her home on a West Texas ranch and supported the next generation of farmers.
body: Audrey Johnson was born in Soper, Oklahoma, on 8 January 1911, the daughter of Joel Anderson Johnson and Winnie Bozarth. She grew up in the southeastern Oklahoma community where her father bought livestock and worked the land. Her brother Joe remained near Boswell and later became Bob Johnson’s father.

On 29 December 1928, Audrey married Riley James King in Paris, Texas. The couple settled in Sterling City, west of San Angelo, where they ranched. Their daughter Bonnie Ruth was born in San Angelo on New Year’s Day 1930.

Audrey and Riley supported 4-H and the Future Farmers of America, organizations that gave local young people a place to learn about agriculture and livestock. Audrey was active in the Church of Christ and taught Bible classes. In 1967 the Kings attended an American Cancer Society meeting in Houston, taking part in sessions on service and public education.

Audrey lived in Sterling City until 1988, then moved to San Angelo. She died there on 7 December 1989 and was buried in the Sterling City cemetery. The 1989 notice names her parents and her husband, connecting the Sterling City family back to Joel and Winnie Johnson in Oklahoma.

stories.title: Bonnie King Alley: from Sterling City to Saudi Arabia
stories.hook: After a West Texas wedding, Bonnie and Gene Alley made a home thousands of miles away on the Arabian Peninsula.
body: Bonnie Ruth King was born on 1 January 1930 in San Angelo, the daughter of Audrey Johnson and Riley King. Raised in Sterling City, she studied at Abilene Christian College and San Angelo Business School and worked for agricultural offices in West Texas. There she met Marvin Eugene “Gene” Alley, a Texas A&M graduate who worked in soil conservation.

At the Sterling City Church of Christ on 6 December 1952, Bonnie and Gene married. Her bridal clothes included a lace and nylon gown and a fingertip veil; she carried a Bible inlaid with mother of pearl, a gift from Gene. The local paper printed her bridal portrait on its front page.

Gene had a job supervising a farm in Saudi Arabia at a place the newspaper spelled “Al Khari,” likely al-Kharj. The paper reported plans for the couple to leave on 12 January 1953. A later family remembrance recalled their journey as immediately after the wedding, so the exact departure date remains uncertain. For Bonnie it was her first airplane journey and her first trip beyond the Oklahoma visits of her childhood.

The Alleys spent a little over two years in Saudi Arabia. They returned to Texas and ranched in Sterling County for about sixteen years. Their son Robert Eugene was born in 1963. The family later moved to Midland, where Gene worked as a land appraiser and Bonnie as a teacher’s aide.

Robert died in 1981, and Gene died in 2000. Bonnie died in San Angelo on 4 January 2012 and was buried at Sterling City. Her life connected an Oklahoma farming family, a West Texas ranching town and an unexpected chapter in Saudi Arabia.

stories.title: Winnie Nelton Beeman and the Wacouta Street family
stories.hook: Census sheets and a Winona address trace Winnie’s household while leaving a question about her earliest name and birth year.
body: Winnie Nelton Beeman was the daughter of George Nelton and Ida Zenk, according to her 1966 family notice. She and Arthur Oscar Beeman raised a family in the Winona area, with periods in nearby Plainview. The family included sons Arthur Chester and Harold Oscar and daughter Berniece May.

The 1910 census recorded Winnie, age twenty-seven, and Arthur in Plainview with their two young sons. By 1930 the couple were in Winona with Harold, Bernice and a grandchild. Arthur died in 1932; by 1950 Winnie was widowed and shared a household with her daughter Bernice, who was working as an assistant cook at a hotel.

A likely earlier record reaches back to 1899: the Wisconsin marriage register identifies a Winona-born bride named Alvina Nelten, daughter of George and Edith, who married blacksmith Arthur O. Beeman at Bluff Siding. The 1900 census then places Alvina and Arthur at 576 Wacouta Street, the address later associated with Winnie. The matching husband, father and address make this a strong possibility, but the different given names and mother’s names leave the identification open. (Lead)

The possible 1900 census entry gives Alvina’s birth as March 1883, and Winnie’s ages in the 1910, 1930 and 1950 censuses are consistent with that year. Her 1966 notice gives 4 March 1882. The exact day and year remain unresolved; the records should be read together rather than treating either date as settled.

Winnie died in Winona on 3 January 1966 and was buried at Woodlawn Cemetery. Her family notice also preserves the names of brothers and sisters scattered across the Winona area, including relatives who do not yet have an established place in the tree.

stories.title: Nel Canfield and the daughters in two censuses
stories.hook: After James Canfield died, two census pages follow his widow and their daughters from Kellogg to Winona.
body: In September 1906, James Garfield Canfield and Helen Heffernan married in Wabasha County, Minnesota. James was a son of John A. Canfield and Anna Hall. His own mother had died when he was an infant, leaving his father to raise him in the Kellogg area.

In 1910 the census taker recorded James, twenty-eight; Helen, twenty-five; their daughter Marion, two; and Maude Hefferman, nineteen, described as James’s sister-in-law. Helen and Maude both reported an Irish-born father and a Minnesota-born mother. A second daughter, Helen Berle, was born on 9 November 1910.
James died on 19 June 1912, aged thirty, leaving Nel with two small daughters. He was buried at St. Agnes Cemetery in Kellogg. The two girls would next appear together in a household in Winona.

By 1920 Tom Miller, twenty-eight, and his wife Nellie, thirty-three, were living in Winona with Marian and Helen Canfield, listed as Tom’s stepdaughters. Helen’s later family notice identifies her as Mrs. Thomas S. Miller, formerly Helen Heffernan, and names both daughters. Together the records follow Nel and the girls into another household after James’s death.

The Heffernan family appears across several records. John and Mary’s 1900 household included Nelly, Kathy, Loy, Maudie and Villy. Helen’s family later named sisters Maude Kling and Catherine Ley and brothers Lloyd and William. Helen’s 1939 Social Security application identifies John H. Heffernan and Mary Shea as her parents; her 1948 death index records Patrick Heffernan and Ellen Shea instead. John and Mary are a probable match, with that conflict still unresolved.

Mary Shea Heffernan died in Winona in March 1903. The family notice names her husband John, five surviving children—Helen, Katie, Loy, Maud and Willie—and her parents, Mr. and Mrs. J. Shea of Kellogg. Her death register indexes her parents as Jermia Shay and Ellen Holliham, both born in Ireland. Mary’s notice also names a brother, P. W. Shea. A 1914 death register for Patrick W. Shea names Jeremiah Shea and Ellen Holland as his parents. The family link is probable and the two readings of Ellen’s surname remain unresolved. Mary’s 1900 census entry gives a Minnesota birth in 1863; her family notice instead gives St. Louis in 1864.

Helen Berle later married Arthur Nelton, a Winona-area carpenter and firefighter. Her sister Marion Canfield married in Winona in 1926 and settled in Wisconsin. Nel died at home in Winona Township in January 1948. Her daughters carried the Canfield and Heffernan family into another generation.

stories.title: Winnie Bozarth and a family across the Red River
stories.hook: Marriage and census records follow Winnie from Texas to a household of children and grandchildren in Choctaw County.
body: On 17 May 1896, Joel A. Johnson and Minnie or Winnie W. Bozarth were married in Lee County, Texas. Their names appear together in the county marriage index. The young couple later crossed the Red River into what became Choctaw County, Oklahoma.

In 1910 Winnie and Joel were living in Oakes Township with five children: Aletha, Porter, George, Willie and Joel, then one year old. The older children were recorded as born in Texas; Willie and little Joel were recorded as born in Oklahoma. Joel Gilbert, the youngest boy, became Rachel’s great-grandfather.

By 1920 another daughter, Audrey, was in the household. The census also listed a two-year-old granddaughter, Lila Smith, and Florence Minton, fifty-eight, described as Joel’s mother-in-law. The wife’s name was indexed as Minnie; the ages and the children’s names connect this household to Winnie and Joel’s 1910 family. Florence is a probable match for Winnie’s mother, although her earlier surname needs further confirmation.

In 1930 Winnie and Joel lived in Boswell with their son Joel Gilbert and their granddaughter Lila, then twelve. Joel worked buying livestock, and the family remained in the Choctaw County communities where the younger children had grown up.

Joel died in 1961. Their shared headstone in Boswell’s Restland Cemetery records Winnie’s dates as 1 July 1881 and 5 April 1969. The records leave questions about Florence’s earlier life and Winnie’s father, but they preserve a picture of several generations living together in the Johnson household.

stories.title: Building a church on Oak Ridge
stories.hook: A gathering in a neighbor’s home became a brick church for the Luxembourg families of Oak Ridge.
body: On 5 December 1875, Catholics living near Oak Ridge in Winona County met at John Speltz’s house to organize a congregation. Their meeting grew into a brick church on the ridge, where many immigrant families had settled.

An 1883 county history credits Peter and John Speltz, Jacob Frisch and other neighbors with helping bring the building to completion. Jacob and his wife Annette Speltz had come from Luxembourg and made their home in the area. The book does not establish how the Speltz men were related to Annette.

The church’s cemetery became a place where several members of the Frisch family were remembered. Its modern burial index lists Jacob and Annette together in lot 49, and Anna, whom the index calls Jacob’s daughter. It also records a young son, Alois, but marks his dates and grave location uncertain.

Jacob died in 1906, four years after Annette. Their son John P. Frisch continued to farm on Oak Ridge, and his daughter Viola later married Edward Rivers. The surviving church history and cemetery index follow the family from an immigrant household to another generation in the Rollingstone area.

stories.title: John Frisch and the farmers’ mutual
stories.hook: A farm insurance officer from Oak Ridge appears in a national banking debate as well as Minnesota newspapers.
body: John P. Frisch farmed the family place at Oak Ridge and worked for a farmers’ mutual insurance company. In January 1911 the Willmar Tribune reported that the Rollingstone Farmers Mutual Fire Insurance Company had held its annual meeting in Winona, paid its debts and retained a $7,000 surplus. John Frisch of Mount Vernon was chosen secretary.

His work for the mutual continued for years. In 1932 he became president of the Minnesota association of mutual insurance companies, according to his family notice. The following January, a different kind of record placed his name in Washington: the Congressional Record listed John Frisch of Rollingstone, secretary of the local mutual, among people whose messages supported the banking bill being debated in the Senate.

The bill, S. 4412, addressed banking and the use of bank assets during the Depression. The record lists Frisch’s name and organization among the senders; it does not print an individual message from him or show him speaking to the Senate. The local farmer’s name survives there alongside the many other businesses and organizations involved in the debate.

John moved from Oak Ridge to Rollingstone around 1929. He died on 16 March 1934. His daughter Viola had married Edward Rivers the previous year, and Edward began work as an insurance agent in Rollingstone in 1934.

stories.title: From Rollingstone to the Mayo Clinic
stories.hook: A Rollingstone physician became a Mayo Clinic consultant and studied digestive disease. His connection to Rachel’s family is still being researched.
body: Andrew Baptiste Rivers was born in Rollingstone, Minnesota, and followed a path into medicine that led him to Rochester. After graduating from St. Francis College in Wisconsin in 1913, he earned his medical degree at Creighton University in Omaha in 1917. He interned at the City and County Hospital in St. Paul and served in the Navy Medical Corps during the First World War.

Rivers joined the Mayo Foundation as a fellow in medicine in 1920. He became an instructor in 1925, an assistant professor in 1932 and an associate professor of medicine in 1947. He was also a consultant in medicine at the Mayo Clinic. His research included digestive disease: a 1933 study he coauthored examined the secretion of pepsin in people with duodenal ulcers and related symptoms.

He died on 3 October 1948. His obituary identifies Angela Rivers as his sister; her 1976 obituary names her parents as John and Bertha Jung Rivers. This supports a connection to the Andrew in John H. Rivers’s 1913 family biography. The dates do not quite agree: the biography gives 10 December 1895, while the university memorial and the 1919 Navy officers’ register give 10 December 1894.

The proposed path from this Rivers family to Rachel also depends on parent links that have not yet been independently established. Until those generations are documented, Andrew’s exact relationship to Rachel remains a research lead.
